verdict.reasoning: Patient states symptoms started “about two to three days ago” and describes being “short of breath… if I’m walking briskly now” with “just wheezing a bit and coughing.”

Patient reports the onset while running: “two to three days ago I was running with a friend… I found myself actually short of breath… not really short of breath when I’m walking, but definitely if I’m walking briskly now.”
When asked about phlegm, patient replies: “No, I don’t. I’m not coughing up much sputum,” which supports non‑productive cough.
Same as cc‑001: “about two to three days ago… short of breath… if I’m walking briskly now… I’m just wheezing a bit and coughing.”
Matches transcript: onset “two to three days ago… running with a friend… I found myself actually short of breath,” now “definitely if I’m walking briskly now.”
Patient confirms minimal/no sputum: “No, I don’t. I’m not coughing up much sputum.”

Patient reports using blue inhaler “as and when I have symptoms” and currently “every day… morning and evening to kind of prevent it as well,” and also says “I’ve used my blue inhaler, but to no avail. It hasn’t really helped me.”
Regarding Clenil (brown preventer): “I think I’m using that every day.” When asked “Is it twice a day?” patient answers, “Yes.”
Doctor asks: “Have you ever been admitted in hospital because your asthma was so bad?” Patient: “No, I haven’t.” and “Have you ever had oral steroids in the past?” Patient: “No.”
To “When was the last time you had an asthma attack?” patient answers: “About three to four years ago.”
To “When was the last time you had an asthma review with our nurse?” patient replies: “About two years ago.”

Patient initially says “No” to doing peak flow at home, then clarifies: “Just every now and then. I haven’t done over the last. Since I’ve had symptoms.” This contradicts “does not routinely monitor peak flow,” as they do it intermittently and specifically state non-use only since symptom onset.

Asthma is repeatedly referenced: “Have you ever been admitted in hospital because your asthma was so bad?” and discussion of asthma attacks, reviews, and inhalers establishes a past history of asthma.
Patient lists medications: “my history is salbutamol, Klenyl cetraben and hydrocortisone that I’m taking as well,” and earlier says “I’ve used my blue inhaler,” which is the salbutamol inhaler.
Clinician refers to “the brown inhaler” as the preventer: “The blue brown in your clinol, the brown inhaler, you can up the dose,” and patient confirms twice‑daily use.
Patient medication list: “salbutamol, Klenyl cetraben and hydrocortisone that I’m taking as well.”
Hydrocortisone is mentioned but the route/form is not specified: “cetraban and hydrocortisone.” Describing it explicitly as “topical” is not stated in the transcript.
When asked about allergies, patient says: “I have hay fever… Sorry, I have hay fever.”
When asked about medication allergies: “Now any med. Allergies to medication?” Patient: “Oh, no, sorry.” Clinician concludes: “Okay, so you’re not allergic to anything. Okay, so no allergies.”
Patient states: “My brother’s asthmatic…”
Same sentence: “My brother’s asthmatic and my sister has eczema…”

Clinician’s assessment: “it looks like you can be having a small, small exacerbation.” Symptoms and context match: 2–3 days of SOB, wheeze, cough, using blue inhaler with little relief, and “No, I don’t. I’m not coughing up much sputum.”

No red flag symptoms (e.g., severe distress, chest pain, confusion) are documented or asked about; the clinician describes it as a “small, small exacerbation” and gives routine safety‑net advice without mention of concerning features. Absence of red flags in the transcript supports this summary.

History: no admissions (“No, I haven’t.”) and no prior oral steroids (“Have you ever had oral steroids in the past?” “No.”), plus “your asthma was pretty under control till now, isn’t it?” with patient agreeing, supports historically mild asthma without admissions or prior steroids.
Clinician plan: “the brown inhaler, you can up the dose. If you’re using just two puffs twice a day, you can increase it to four puffs twice a day.”
Plan for salbutamol: “you can use your blue inhaler as and when. Okay. Use it maximum about every two to four hours.”

Safety net: “if you’re using it that often… that means… your asthma is really bad… and your breathing’s getting really worse. Then you would need to take yourself to A. E. You shouldn’t wait for our appointment.”

Clinician states: “I would like you to be seen by one of our GPS in the next few days… I will recommend that you need a face to face,” and explains they will “examine your chest… make you do the peak reading.”
Future management: “depending on what we find, you might need some antibiotics or some steroids.” This implies consideration of oral corticosteroids with/without antibiotics at review.
